Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Making any plans for the future

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.item: Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
issues.explanation: 'Irritability' is not a threat appraisal/perception item; it reflects arousal/behavioral dysregulation and fits better outside the Threat node. In this profile, the other Threat items are coherent terrorism-related hypervigilance/safety behaviors ('Scanning Exits', 'Back to Wall'), so this item is internally mismatched within the node and weakly aligned with the formulation in which Memory-linked threat should reflect perceived current danger rather than aggressive behavior.

vignette:
Daniel was 33, a single African man who had built his life around tailoring work in the city, measuring hems and pinning seams for clients who came and went through the small shop where he spent most of his days. Before the bombing, he had been known as steady and meticulous, the kind of tailor who remembered fittings and deadlines. That changed after the day of the terrorist attack, when he was caught near a crowded public place and everything around him turned to smoke, shouting, and motion. In the confusion there had been bodies rushing in different directions, and Daniel later found that parts of that day were simply missing from him no matter how much he tried to reach for them. He could recall the blast in fragments, and other moments came back with such force that they felt like a film he was forced to watch again and again: the sound, the panic, the sense of danger spreading through the crowd. At other times, he could describe what happened almost without feeling anything at all, as if it had happened to someone else and he was only repeating the facts.

In the weeks that followed, Daniel began to live as though danger might break in at any moment. The first thing he did whenever he entered a room, a bus, a restaurant, or even the front area of his own shop was to look for the exits. He would not sit unless he could place his back against a wall and see the whole space in front of him. In the tailoring shop, this meant choosing the chair closest to the wall and scanning the doorway each time it opened, which made it hard for him to settle with customers. He was constantly watchful, noticing every sudden sound in the street, every raised voice, every unfamiliar movement near the entrance. Clients sometimes noticed that he seemed distracted or tense, but Daniel felt he was simply making sure he would not be caught unaware again. He was certain that being alert was the only reason he could still get through the day.

As the months passed, Daniel started spending long stretches on his phone, scrolling aimlessly, playing games, or drifting across the internet until the hours disappeared. When the screen was in his hands, his mind did not have to go back to the event. He also began picking arguments and creating drama with people around him, especially when the silence became too heavy or when he felt himself drifting into memories he did not want. He would bring up small grievances with relatives or customers, not because the issues mattered so much, but because conflict gave him something else to focus on. He had also stopped making plans for the future. He did not talk about saving money, expanding the shop, or thinking ahead to marriage or family the way others expected him to. In his own mind, planning felt pointless and exposed; he could not trust that he would do the right thing if another crisis came, and he had come to believe that the ground under his life was not secure enough for promises.

Daniel’s beliefs about himself had become harsh and fixed. He spoke of not belonging anywhere, even though he lived among family and worked among familiar people. He said it in a quiet, matter-of-fact way, as if stating something he had already tested and found true. He felt weak because he had not been able to stop what happened, and because afterward he could not force himself to think or live as he used to. There were moments when the memory replayed so vividly that he felt trapped inside it, and other moments when the same memory seemed empty of feeling, which unsettled him in a different way. Either way, it left him uneasy and on guard. In the shop, he became known for pausing at the sound of footsteps outside and turning quickly when someone entered too fast. If he was seated, he shifted his chair until he could see the full room.

He came for help after his avoidance and tension had begun to shape his life in ways he could no longer ignore. He was tired of losing hours to his phone, of arguments he started just to keep his mind busy, and of watching himself withdraw from any thought of a future. What brought him in was the sense that he was no longer living fully in his own shop, in his own body, or in his own life. What he feared most was that the memories and the constant watchfulness would never let him belong anywhere again, and what he hoped for, cautiously, was some way to feel safe enough to work, move, and think ahead without waiting for the next explosion.
